REUTERS/Stephane Mahe The European Union has imposed a new round of sanctions targeting the shipowners, vessel managers, insurers and financial networks supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, expanding its efforts to disrupt the maritime infrastructure behind Russian oil exports. The measures announced Monday add 12 individuals and 101 entities to the EU’s sanctions list, including companies based in the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Seychelles and China that Brussels says are involved in transporting or trading Russian oil. The latest designations go beyond individual tankers to target the companies and people that own, manage, insure and finance their operations. Among those sanctioned are Russian nationals Igor Konfino and Daniil Mosin, identified by the EU as managers of White Agate Marine, Citrine Marine and Serpentine Marine, companies that own vessels already subject to European sanctions. According to the EU’s Official Journal , several of those vessels were previously owned by Russian shipping giant Sovcomflot or associated companies. The EU says the ownership and management structures maintain links to Sovcomflot while operating tankers engaged in high-risk shipping practices. The sanctions also target a network of Dubai-based companies involved in Russian oil transportation, including Lidoil DMCC, Spikoil DMCC, Lynx Ship Management, Stalwart Shipmanagement, Grace Shipmanagement and Greenlight Shipmanagement. EU officials say Lidoil manages tankers carrying Russian crude and petroleum products through shell companies, while Spikoil operates vessels on its behalf. The listings also expose financial connections supporting those operations. Moscow-based Lead Capital, an affiliate of Lidoil, was sanctioned for helping raise financing in Russia to support the tanker network. Marine insurance is another target. The EU designated Moscow-based Balance Insurance, which it says provided coverage to the oil tanker GARUDA , a vessel previously sanctioned over high-risk shipping practices while transporting Russian crude. The inclusion of an insurer highlights the broader effort to restrict the services that allow sanctioned tankers to remain in operation, even when individual vessels have already been blacklisted. Brussels also sanctioned JSC Petersburg Oil Terminal, which operates an oil terminal in the St. Petersburg region, extending the measures to infrastructure supporting Russia’s energy exports. The maritime designations form part of a wider sanctions package targeting Russia’s energy and financial sectors. Nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions were also added to the list as the EU seeks to limit Moscow’s access to financing. Under the measures, designated individuals and companies face asset freezes, while EU persons and businesses are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them, directly or indirectly. Listed individuals are also subject to EU travel bans. articles.summary: Two tankers were reportedly attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, November 16, with both incidents resulting in engine-room fires and one vessel left disabled, according to separate warnings...

REUTERS/Stringer Two tankers were reportedly attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, November 16, with both incidents resulting in engine-room fires and one vessel left disabled, according to separate warnings issued by United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). The latest incident occurred at approximately 1900 UTC, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. According to UKMTO, a third party reported that a tanker transiting the strategic waterway had been attacked, leaving the vessel disabled and causing a fire in its engine room. The crew was reported safe, although the extent of damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. Earlier Monday, at approximately 0558 UTC, the company security officer of another tanker reported that the vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz. The impact sparked a fire in the engine room, according to UKMTO. No casualties were reported, and all crew members were accounted for. The vessel’s condition and any potential environmental damage remained under assessment. The incidents follow another reported tanker attack on Sunday, November 15, when Indian shipping authorities notified UKMTO that a vessel had been attacked while traveling eastbound through the Arabian Gulf toward the Strait of Hormuz. All crew members were reported safe. The latest attacks come amid a sustained campaign of violence against commercial shipping in and around the waterway. JMIC reported five attacks off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula since November 1 and said maritime traffic remained substantially below prewar levels. The center also reported approximately 227 commercial vessels stationary at major anchorages east of the Strait of Hormuz, including Fujairah, Khor Fakkan, Sohar and Musandam, as restricted transit continues to create a persistent backlog. The latest JMIC assessment recorded 83 U.S.-facilitated transits between November 12 and 14, while separately tracked, non-facilitated commercial traffic remained at single-digit to low-double-digit levels per day. Those figures cover different vessel populations and should not be treated as directly comparable. UKMTO has not identified the vessels involved in Monday’s reported attacks or attributed responsibility. Authorities are investigating both incidents, and vessels operating in the region have been advised to exercise caution and report suspicious activity. articles.title: Why the carrier with the shortest terminal wait isn’t always the fastest option
articles.summary: Peak season volume has to land somewhere. The usual inputs to that decision are cost, space, and a general sense of which carrier “runs well” on a given route. Reliability gets discussed, but rarely checked against anything concrete, because container terminal performance data has not been easily compiled across...
articles.body: Why the carrier with the shortest terminal wait isn’t always the fastest option in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 Peak season volume has to land somewhere. The usual inputs to that decision are cost, space, and a general sense of which carrier “runs well” on a given route. Reliability gets discussed, but rarely checked against anything concrete, because container terminal performance data has not been easily compiled across carriers at the same set of ports. Here’s what happens once it is. The questions behind every port congestion decision A BCO deciding which carrier should absorb extra peak season volume is asking two distinct questions at once. 1. How often is this carrier delayed getting into berth at the ports I care about? 2. Once it’s alongside, how long does it take before the vessel sails again? Most routing conversations only ever look at the first question, usually filtered through reputation rather than a number. The second question barely surfaces at all, even though it matters just as much for container shipping schedule reliability. An example in Terminal Activity Using the Terminal Activity workspace in Container Intelligence, we can take four carrier groups calling San Pedro, Seattle, and Tacoma on vessels above 5,000 TEU, benchmarked against each other from January through September 2026: • MSC • CMA CGM • China COSCO Shipping • Hapag-Lloyd MSC is the dominant carrier at these ports by volume, with 122 terminal calls across the period, more than the other three carrier groups combined. CMA CGM runs 44 calls, China COSCO Shipping 27, and Hapag-Lloyd the fewest at 20. Looking at waiting rate alone, Hapag-Lloyd looks like the standout for the share of calls that experienced any wait at all. It averages 43.5% across the nine months, well below the other three. China COSCO Shipping sits at the other end, averaging 80.6%, the highest of the group. MSC and CMA CGM land in between, at 70.2% and 67.2%. Average waiting time per call tells a similar story on the surface. Hapag-Lloyd averages just 3.3 hours of waiting per call across the period, the lowest of the four. China COSCO Shipping averages 6.4 hours, CMA CGM 8.3 hours, and MSC the highest at 13.0 hours. On those two metrics alone, Hapag-Lloyd reads as the carrier least likely to sit waiting for a berth at these ports. While a useful finding, it’s not the whole picture of container port performance at these three gateways. The port call figures that change the answer Waiting rate and waiting time only measure one part of a vessel’s time at port, the part before it reaches berth. What happens once it’s alongside is a separate question, and it’s where the picture flips. Hapag-Lloyd’s average berth stay across the nine months runs to 112.8 hours. It shows up consistently, every month from January through September, running noticeably longer than any of the other three carrier groups, which range from roughly 36 to 62 hours on average. Put the two halves of the port call together, the wait to get to berth and the stay once there, and the ranking that looked settled a moment ago reverses. This is container terminal benchmarking at its most useful, two metrics that individually point one way and combine to point the other: Hapag-Lloyd: 3.3 hours waiting plus 112.8 hours at berth, a total of roughly 116 hours per call. CMA CGM: 8.3 hours waiting plus 61.7 hours at berth, roughly 70 hours per call. MSC: 13.0 hours waiting plus 42.1 hours at berth, roughly 55 hours per call. China COSCO Shipping: 6.4 hours waiting plus 35.9 hours at berth, roughly 42 hours per call, the shortest total of the four. The carrier with the best waiting numbers has, by a wide margin, the longest total time in port once berth stay is counted. The carrier with the worst waiting rate, China COSCO Shipping, where 8 in 10 calls experience some wait, comes out with the shortest combined cycle, because both its waits and its berth stays run short. None of that is a claim about why Hapag-Lloyd’s berth stays run long, whether it’s vessel size, cargo mix, terminal handling priority, or something else entirely. The data doesn’t say. It does however show that a carrier can look clearly best on one measure of container terminal performance and clearly worst on another, and a routing decision made on only one of those measures would have missed the part that matters for schedule reliability. The call volume caveat Call volume differs a lot across these four carrier groups, and that matters for how much weight any single month’s number should carry in a container terminal benchmarking exercise. In some months, Hapag-Lloyd’s call count drops to just one. A one-call month that happens to post a 0% waiting rate, as Hapag-Lloyd does in March and June, is a real data point, but it’s not the same kind of evidence as MSC’s waiting rate in the same month, built from 13 calls. The nine-month average smooths this out somewhat, but a BCO using this data to shape an actual peak season decision should look at the call volume behind each number, not just the number itself. What this changes about the port routing decision A routing decision made on waiting rate or waiting time alone would have pointed toward Hapag-Lloyd. A decision made on total time in port, which is arguably the number that determines container shipping schedule reliability, points toward China COSCO Shipping instead, at least across this period and this set of ports. That’s not a recommendation to pick one carrier over another in general. It’s a demonstration of why the question “which carrier should absorb our peak season volume” doesn’t have a single right metric to check it against, and why container port performance needs more than one lens before a decision gets made. A few things follow from having both halves of the picture available at once: • Waiting rate and waiting time answer how predictable it is to get into berth. Berth stay answers how long cargo actually sits once it’s there. A peak season decision needs both, not one standing in for the other. • Volume matters alongside the averages. A carrier running 122 calls in a period, as MSC does here, is a different kind of data point than one running 20, even when both produce a clean average. • The best carrier depends on where the risk sits. Specifically, which part of the port call threatens the schedule commitment, getting delayed before berth, or getting delayed at berth. Where this leaves a BCO planning around terminal congestion This comparison has historically been hard to put together across several carriers and ports at once, which is why it gets skipped. But with container terminal performance data, that comparison is no longer something a BCO has to take on faith. Here are three things worth checking before locking in a routing decision: 1. Look at waiting rate and waiting time alongside berth stay, not instead of it. One half tells you how predictable it is to get into berth, the other tells you how long cargo sits once it’s there, and a routing decision needs the full port call in view, not just the part that’s easiest to find. 2. Check berth stay before treating strong waiting numbers as proof of a faster overall port call. A carrier that waits the least to get to berth can still have the longest total time in port. 3. Weigh every monthly figure against the call volume behind it. A carrier running a handful of calls a month and one running more than a dozen aren’t offering the same strength of evidence, even when their averages land on the same chart. The carrier that ends up absorbing peak season volume should be the one that performs best on whichever part of the port call actually drives the commitment being made, not the one with the single most flattering number on the first chart pulled up. articles.summary: A potential shift in US policy guidance could trigger new catalysts for the global shipping markets in the years to come. articles.body: New US Policy Priorities Could Shape Future Shipping Markets in Hellenic Shipping News 17/11/2026 A potential shift in US policy guidance could trigger new catalysts for the global shipping markets in the years to come. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “the Democratic Party’s victory in the US midterm elections, securing control of both chambers of Congress from January 2027, is expected to influence Washington’s foreign, energy, trade and maritime policies. Democrats will gain greater leverage over legislation, government spending and congressional oversight. Beyond these institutional powers, the election outcome itself could prompt President Trump to reassess certain policy priorities, even without direct Democratic pressure, as the administration considers the political and economic implications of the result. Nevertheless, Trump retains substantial executive authority, and the extent of any policy adjustments remains uncertain”. Source: Intermodal shipbroker According to Mr. Nikos Tagoulis, Head of Research Department with Intermodal, “among the issues with the most immediate implications for shipping is the conflict involving Iran. Democrats are expected to intensify pressure for diplomatic de-escalation and greater congressional oversight of military operations, potentially supporting efforts to restore safe navigation through Hormuz. However, ending military operations, securing maritime passage and adjusting sanctions on Iranian petroleum remain separate policy decisions, with progress dependent on negotiations between Washington and Tehran”. “Any sustained improvement in maritime security around Hormuz could have significant implications for energy and commodity trade. A reopening of the Strait could facilitate the recovery of Middle Eastern exports, easing energy prices, war-risk premiums and transportation costs. Qatar’s LNG exports could gradually recover, although the extent and timing of production restoration remain uncertain following Iranian strikes on liquefaction infrastructure. A recovery in cargo volumes could support tanker demand, while the normalization of trading patterns and vessel availability could moderate exceptionally high freight rates and reduce ton mile demand. For dry bulk, some of the most notable market effects could include a recovery in regional fertilizer exports, while the resumption of LNG exports and lower gas prices could reduce gas-to-coal switching and thermal coal imports in some markets, potentially weighing on thermal coal trade”, Mr. Tagoulis said. “Black Sea represents another area of interest for shipping. Democrats have prioritized increased assistance to Ukraine, although greater congressional support would not necessarily accelerate a ceasefire, with any lasting settlement dependent on developments between Russia and Ukraine. For shipowners, the restoration of reliable commercial navigation, port operations and export corridors would remain central to any agreement”, he added. According to Mr. Tagoulis, “beyond these geopolitical developments, the Democratic victory could influence US trade policy, with Democrats potentially favouring more selective tariffs, closer cooperation with traditional allies and targeted measures supporting strategic US industries, rather than the broad-based tariffs introduced under President Trump. In the maritime sector, the suspension of US port fees affecting Chinese-built and Chinese-linked vessels has been extended until 10 January 2027, shortly after the new Democratic Congress takes office, potentially prompting early congressional scrutiny of its scope and implementation, although final decisions remain with the administration. Furthermore, maritime decarbonization represents another area where Democratic influence could become more pronounced. Democrats generally favour cleaner energy and stronger international environmental cooperation and could advocate renewed US engagement with the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, while also promoting greater investment in alternative marine fuels, lower-emission vessels and greener shipping practices”. Source: Intermodal shipbroker “These environmental priorities could also shape domestic US energy policy, with potential consequences for seaborne energy trade. Democrats may seek to expand renewable energy while advocating greater environmental scrutiny of future offshore oil exploration and new LNG export authorizations, potentially influencing the longer-term outlook for US fossil-fuel production and exports. Meanwhile, the Jones Act and efforts to revitalize domestic shipbuilding appear to retain bipartisan support, suggesting greater continuity in US maritime industrial policy. With the current Jones Act waiver due to expire on 15 November, attention could also turn to the potential extension of exemptions”, Tagoulis noted. Intermodal’s analyst concluded that “overall, the Democratic victory could gradually influence the direction of US foreign, trade, energy and maritime policies, although the immediate implications for shipping will remain closely tied to geopolitical developments and the administration’s policy decisions. A more comprehensive shift could emerge from 2029 if Democrats also secure the presidency in the November 2028 election”. articles.title: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping?
articles.summary: Many ships carrying global trade today will be operating well into the 2030s, yet the transition to alternative fuels takes time. Of the near-zero emission fuel production capacity estimated to be needed by 2030 only around 4% has reached a final investment decision. Worse, alternative-fuel-capable vessel orders fell...
articles.body: Onboard carbon capture: a practical pathway for shipping? in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 M any ships carrying global trade today will be operating well into the 2030s, yet the transition to alternative fuels takes time. Of the near-zero emission fuel production capacity estimated to be needed by 2030 only around 4% has reached a final investment decision. Worse, alternative-fuel-capable vessel orders fell from 45% of contracted tonnage in 2024 to 37% in 2025. This means the global fleet will remain dependent on fossil fuels, or their bio- or e- equivalents, for years to come and must find novel ways to reduce emissions. Energy-efficiency measures reduce fuel consumption, but even those more efficient crossings will continue to produce carbon emissions. A potential role opens for onboard carbon capture and storage (oCCS). By capturing CO₂ from engine exhausts before it reaches the atmosphere, oCCS could help vessels that cannot yet switch to zero- or near-zero emission fuels drastically reduce their emissions. Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt From first installations to commercial use Early commercial installations show oCCS moving beyond concept and pilot-scale development, with amine-based post-combustion capture emerging as the most mature marine option. This is currently the only technology with classed commercial installations, where full-scale systems capture around 30% to 40% of CO₂ emissions. Larger pilots target about 70%. Eastern Pacific Shipping’s Pacific Cobalt became the first classed commercial oCCS installation in 2024 under LR’s Emission Abatement Carbon Capture & Storage (EACCS) (Amine, HFO) class notation, while Solvang’s Clipper Eris is testing a full-scale system designed to capture around 70% of the CO₂ produced by its main engine. These projects add to the growing evidence that oCCS can operate at commercial scale, but its wider value depends on the emissions reductions achieved in practice. That depends partly on the energy needed to operate the system, which can increase fuel consumption by 15% to 30% in current applications. A 70% gross capture with a 15% fuel penalty would deliver an estimated tank-to-wake CO₂ reduction of around 44%, although waste-heat recovery could reduce that penalty. The resulting emissions reduction, cost and operational impact will vary between ships, making vessel suitability central to the business case. Finding the right ships Panos Mitrou, LR Senior Vice President of Shipping Strategy states: “Onboard carbon capture has the potential to become an important part of shipping’s decarbonisation toolkit. For the right vessel types and trades, it offers a realistic pathway to reducing CO₂ emissions and managing carbon costs while fuel supply chains, infrastructure and regulations continue to evolve.” The strongest opportunities for oCCS are likely to be those vessels with sufficient remaining trading life and space for the equipment. The business case will also depend on how and where these vessels operate. For example, medium range and chemical tankers trading on EEA routes have frequent port calls, offering opportunities to offload captured CO₂ while EU carbon-price exposure increases the value of reducing emissions. Panos Mitrou, Senior Vice President, Shipping Strategy, LR For LNG-fuelled vessels and LNG carriers, cold energy released during LNG vaporisation can help liquefy captured CO₂, reducing additional power requirements. Short-sea and feeder vessels could also benefit from predictable routes and regular opportunities to offload. The case for oCCS therefore depends on the technology fitting a vessel’s operating and commercial conditions. Without these or similar conditions, the case weakens. Ships with limited trading life, little carbon-price exposure or poor access to offloading facilities will be less likely to justify the investment. Access to offloading is another critical factor because onboard storage is limited, setting a limit on how long the system can operate before captured CO₂ must be removed. Voyage length and offloading opportunities therefore directly affect how much CO₂ can ultimately be captured, making where and how a vessel operates as important as what can be installed onboard. The decisive challenge lies ashore For oCCS to deliver its intended benefits, captured CO₂ must enter a transport and storage network leading to permanent storage or an eligible use. Limited port reception infrastructure is a constraint, with few ports able to receive ship-captured liquefied CO₂. Many existing facilities are designed for food-grade CO₂ that may not suit exhaust-derived streams. Development is furthest ahead in north-west Europe, supported by emerging North Sea transport and storage networks, but access remains limited elsewhere. The emissions benefit must also be recognised within relevant regulatory frameworks. The EU ETS can recognise captured CO₂ that reaches qualifying permanent storage or utilisation, while FuelEU Maritime does not yet include oCCS in its greenhouse-gas intensity calculations. The IMO is still developing a global framework covering safety, testing, verification and carbon accounting. Practically, the success of oCCS depends on infrastructure and regulation developing alongside the technology. Entering an oCCS world oCCS could offer an emissions-reduction pathway for suitable vessels using fossil fuels or their artificial equivalents as the transition to zero and near-zero emission fuels develops. But there are constraints. Success depends on matching effective capture technology to ships with enough trading life remaining and suitable trading patterns, to form a strong commercial case. Regular offloading access and supporting transport and storage infrastructure must be developed to connect captured CO₂ to permanent storage or an eligible use. Regulation also needs to recognise the resulting emissions reduction, to help create a working carbon economy. Where these technical, operational, commercial, infrastructure and regulatory conditions align, oCCS could help bridge the gap between a carbon-intensive present and a carbon-neutral future. For more information, read the full report Applying Onboard Carbon Capture & Storage to existing ships, which examines where oCCS could work as a retrofit and which ships and trades are best suited to the technology. articles.summary: Cargo securing is a core part of safe operations, and failures can put seafarers, ships and the marine environment at risk. articles.body: Cargo securing compliance starts on deck, not in the manual in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 C argo securing is a core part of safe operations, and failures can put seafarers, ships and the marine environment at risk. That is why cargo securing is the focus of this year’s Concentrated Inspection Campaign (CIC), run jointly by the Tokyo Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the Paris MoU from 1 September to 30 November 2026. Port State Control (PSC) officers will record any deficiencies, and certain shortcomings may result in the ship’s detention. Shipowners and operators will want to prioritize cargo securing while inspections are underway, but good practice matters on every voyage, not only during a campaign. Compliance protects seafarers and ships, and it also protects the bottom line. Deficiencies can raise a ship’s risk profile and lead to more frequent inspections or other penalties. Detention can also cause reputational damage, knock-on schedule changes, and delays that may lead to loss-of-hire costs. Using a questionnaire, inspectors will check compliance with the cargo loading, stowage, and securing requirements of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The questions cover the ship’s Cargo Securing Manual (CSM), crew familiarity with it, the condition of securing equipment, documentation and heavy-weather procedures. Several of these questions go beyond the condition of the equipment. They ask whether the CSM is being complied with, whether cargo has been secured throughout the voyage, and whether heavy-weather procedures have been followed. Answering them depends as much on procedure and record-keeping as on hardware. Sami Koponen Digital tools such as NAPA Checklist and NAPA Logbook support this procedural and record-keeping side of compliance. They help shipowners and operators show that the crew’s actual practice reflects the CSM and that the crew understands the full required process; that securing inspections and maintenance are carried out and accurately recorded, in the form inspectors expect to see; and that the crew follows and logs heavy-weather procedures in the Safety Management System (SMS). Tommi Vihavainen Turning cargo securing compliance into daily practice These digital tools do not replace the CSM or the SMS. They turn existing, approved procedures into guided, recorded routines that the crew follows. In short, they close the gap between an approved procedure on paper and a crew that demonstrably follows it, with the records to prove it. Digitalization can also ease the administrative load on board, giving crews back time and headspace for safety-critical work. A World Maritime University survey of more than 4,000 seafarers, published in January 2026, found that 32.8% were experiencing severe or potentially dangerous levels of work-related stress, with ship inspections and onboard administrative duties ranked as their top two stressors. NAPA Checklist was developed in collaboration with officers and crew from cruise and expedition operators, like HX Expeditions, to reflect crews’ actual processes and needs. It walks crew through each procedure in the correct order and records every action automatically with a timestamp and the name of the person who completed it. Completed tasks then feed directly to NAPA Logbook, eliminating duplicate data entry. NAPA Logbook was introduced across 20 Anthony Veder vessels, and the first wave of engine-room logbook automation saved 8,000 hours across the fleet. Overall, it reduced administrative time by an average of 14%, more than 2,000 hours per vessel annually. Automation has reduced manual data entry, validation has reduced corrections, and information can be entered once and reused for multiple purposes. Ultimately, safety is not just about having the right processes in a manual, but also about ensuring they are thoroughly understood, followed, and reported on, not only during inspection periods but also during day-to-day operations. Inspections will remain a fact of life at sea, but they don’t need to be a source of added pressure for a crew. When procedures are built into the way crews already work, and the records are created as the work is done, an inspection becomes a check on existing practice rather than a scramble for evidence. That benefits crews and operators alike, during this campaign and long after it ends. Source: By Tommi Vihavainen, Director, Development and Product Owner – Logbook, Safety Solutions, NAPA & Sami Koponen, Product Owner, NAPA Checklist, Safety Solutions, NAPA Tops 2026-11-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: That is why cargo securing is the focus of this year’s Concentrated Inspection Campaign (CIC), run jointly by the Tokyo Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the Paris MoU from 1 September to 30 November 2026.
Port State Control (PSC) officers will record any deficiencies, and certain shortcomings may result in the ship’s detention.
Shipowners and operators will want to prioritize cargo securing while inspections are underway, but good practice matters on every voyage, not only during a campaign.

articles.title: ICS Chair warns rising geopolitical risks threaten global trade and freedom of navigation at Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit
articles.summary: The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) has called for renewed international commitment to freedom of navigation and the rules-based maritime system, warning that growing geopolitical tensions and fragmentation are creating significant risks for global trade. Speaking at the third Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade...
articles.body: ICS Chair warns rising geopolitical risks threaten global trade and freedom of navigation at Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) has called for renewed international commitment to freedom of navigation and the rules-based maritime system, warning that growing geopolitical tensions and fragmentation are creating significant risks for global trade. Speaking at the third Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit, hosted by ICS in collaboration with the Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region’s Transport and Logistics Bureau and the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, ICS Chairman John Denholm highlighted the increasingly interconnected nature of geopolitical, economic and maritime risks. John Denholm, Chairman of the International Chamber of Shipping Addressing the 250 plus delegates John Denholm, Chairman of the International Chamber of Shipping, said: “We are seeing geopolitical tensions reshape trade flows, conflicts disrupting established shipping routes, greater competition between major economies, and a growing tendency towards unilateral measures and regional regulation. At the same time, the global economy is asking shipping to undertake a major energy transition while continuing to provide the reliable, affordable transport on which international commerce depends. This matters because shipping does not operate in isolation. It is the connective tissue of the global economy. Around 90% of world trade by volume is carried by sea, meaning that the security and efficiency of maritime transport is inseparable from ensuring people across the world have food to eat, the essential goods needed to survive, and the energy to heat their homes.” Under the theme Navigating Risk – Partnering for Resilience, the Summit brought together government representatives, policymakers and senior industry figures to examine how international trade can remain resilient in an increasingly uncertain global environment. Speakers included: • Paul Chan Mo Po, GBM, GBS, MH, JP, Financial Secretary, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR • Mable Chan, JP, Secretary for Transport and Logistics, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR • Emma Roberts, Vice President Maritime and Supply Chain Excellence, BHP, Singapore • Nick Brown, CEO, Lloyd’s Register, United Kingdom Paul Chan Mo-po, GBM, GBS, MH, JP, Financial Secretary, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR told the conference: “This year has shown how much change trade can absorb. To shape the changes ahead is a task for partnership. Hong Kong began as a harbour. What it offers today is what stands behind the harbour: rules that endure, time that is saved, and services and people that add value to every voyage.” Paul Chan Mo Po, GBM, GBS, MH, JP, Financial Secretary, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR Disruptions to established maritime routes, conflicts and growing protectionism have demonstrated how quickly regional instability can translate into higher shipping costs, delayed deliveries and pressure on supply chains around the world. Concluding the conference Mable Chan, JP, Secretary for Transport and Logistics, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR said: “Throughout today’s discussions under the theme “Navigating Risk – Partnering for Resilience”, one truth has stood out: in an era of redrawn trade lanes, geopolitical friction and climate urgency, no single jurisdiction or sector can build supply chain resilience alone. Resilience is not merely about enduring disruption; it is about adapting through strategic partnership, shared investment, and forward-looking innovation.” Mable Chan, JP, Secretary for Transport and Logistics, The Government of the Hong Kong SAR The Summit concluded with a call for continued dialogue and practical cooperation between governments and the maritime industry to safeguard freedom of navigation, protect seafarers, and ensure that international shipping can continue to support global economic prosperity. Source: International Chamber of Shipping 2026-11-17 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: OceanScore advances port emissions intelligence ambitions through agreement with RightShip on MEP customer portfolio
articles.summary: OceanScore has signed an agreement with RightShip to assume responsibility for the customer portfolio of RightShip’s Maritime Emissions Portal (MEP), marking a further step in OceanScore’s ambition to establish a global standard for port emissions intelligence and significantly expanding OceanScore’s reach in the...
articles.body: OceanScore advances port emissions intelligence ambitions through agreement with RightShip on MEP customer portfolio in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 OceanScore has signed an agreement with RightShip to assume responsibility for the customer portfolio of RightShip’s Maritime Emissions Portal (MEP), marking a further step in OceanScore’s ambition to establish a global standard for port emissions intelligence and significantly expanding OceanScore’s reach in the global ports sector. The agreement combines RightShip’s established relationships with port emission customers and OceanScore’s expertise in maritime emissions intelligence, creating opportunities to expand the global reach of its PortView platform and strengthen the solutions available to ports worldwide. RightShip CEO Steen Lund commented: “Following a thorough evaluation of OceanScore’s solutions, we concluded that the company was best suited to support RightShip’s Maritime Emissions Portal customers with their future port emissions monitoring and reporting needs. As RightShip continues to focus on our core strengths in maritime safety and risk intelligence, we remain committed to supporting our customers through this transition and ensuring they have a clear pathway forward. OceanScore’s established relationships with ports, strong technological capabilities and expertise in port emissions intelligence give us confidence in its ability to support customers who choose to transition to PortView” Building towards a global standard for port emissions intelligence OceanScore’s PortView platform provides ports with actionable vessel intelligence, supporting emissions monitoring, environmental reporting, shore power planning and alternative fuel readiness. The agreement further extends PortView’s international reach, building on OceanScore’s established relationships with the global port community through its work supporting port incentive schemes, including the Environmental Ship Index (ESI) and Environmental Port Index (EPI), as well as initiatives addressing underwater radiated noise (URN). OceanScore serves as the global administrator of ESI, developed and owned by the International Association of Ports and Harbors (IAPH), which enables ports to identify and reward vessels that exceed environmental regulatory requirements. From January 2027, OceanScore will also support EPI alongside ESI on a shared technical platform under the IAPH umbrella. While ESI assesses a vessel’s overall environmental performance, EPI focuses on its environmental performance during individual port calls. Together, these solutions reflect OceanScore’s growing role in supporting ports with consistent environmental data, performance assessment and effective incentive schemes, helping them make informed decisions and advance their environmental objectives. This ambition received further backing in 2026, when OceanScore was awarded a grant from the Portuguese government to support the development of a global standard for port emissions intelligence. Albrecht Grell, Managing Director of OceanScore, said: “RightShip has built strong relationships with ports through MEP, and we are pleased to have been selected to take this offering forward. Their confidence in OceanScore is a strong endorsement of our approach and an important step towards establishing a global standard for port emissions intelligence.” “Through PortView and our work with ESI and EPI, we are already supporting ports in turning environmental data into meaningful action. By bringing MEP into our offering, we can extend these benefits to more ports worldwide, providing consistent, reliable insights to support emissions reduction, environmental reporting and long-term infrastructure planning.” Supporting ports worldwide OceanScore and RightShip will work closely to ensure continuity for existing MEP customers as the offering transitions to OceanScore. For port authorities, the agreement aims to ensure continuity in emissions monitoring while creating opportunities to benefit from OceanScore’s broader expertise in environmental intelligence and performance management. This will support ports in measuring and understanding vessel emissions, assessing environmental performance and making informed decisions on emissions reduction and infrastructure investments. By combining MEP’s established presence with PortView and OceanScore’s cooperation with IAPH on environmental incentive schemes, the agreement represents another step towards a globally consistent approach to measuring and managing port emissions. articles.body: LNG Bunker Snapshot: Singapore price drops as JKM moves to January in International Shipping News 17/11/2026 ARA Rotterdam’s LNG bunker price has fallen by $8/mt week-on-week to $1,630/mt. TTF fell early in the week as hopes of progress in US-Iran peace talks eased worries over the Middle East, the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) said. “Expectations for an easing of Middle East tensions have reduced concerns over energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, taking some of the geopolitical premium out of European gas prices,” two analysts from ING Bank noted. TTF then rose from 10 November on colder weather in Northwest Europe, unplanned maintenance at Norway’s Troll and Asgard gas fields and slower LNG arrivals in Europe, JOGMEC added. EU-wide underground gas storage stood at 70.8% on 13 November, down from 73% the previous weekend and 14.6% below the level recorded in the same period last year, according to data from Gas Infrastructure Europe. Singapore Singapore’s LNG bunker price has fallen by far more than ARA’s, flipping from a $109/mt premium over ARA a week ago to a $41/mt discount. Most of Singapore’s fall, $91/mt, came as the front-month JKM contract moved from December to January. January JKM stands at $29.60/MMBtu ($1,539/mt), and Singapore’s bunker premium over it at $0.96/MMBtu ($50/mt). “North Asia LNG prices remained under pressure after Qatar, the world’s second-largest exporter of LNG, said it’s seeking to export more LNG through the Strait of Hormuz,” said ANZ Bank senior commodity strategist Daniel Hynes. “Natural gas prices in… Asia were dragged lower by the selloff in the oil market. This was compounded by signs of weaker Chinese interest,” Hynes added. In other LNG bunker news, Swedish gas firm Nordion Energi has installed a new 500 cbm liquefied biomethane (LBM) storage tank at its liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg. US LNG bunker supplier REV LNG has completed the first LNG bunker operation at the Port of Davisville in Rhode Island, delivering by truck to Siem Car Carriers’ vehicle carrier Aristotle. Singapore-based Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS) has bunkered its vehicle carrier Lake Victoria with LNG by truck at the same port, its first truck-to-ship delivery. articles.title: Shipyard Profile: Joey D'Isernia and Eastern Shipbuilding Group
articles.summary: With three shipbuilding facilities, 1,300 employees and a diversified orderbook extending into the next decade, Eastern Shipbuilding Group (ESG) is well positioned to benefit from renewed investment in America's maritime industrial base. CEO Joey D'Isernia discusses the company's growth…
articles.body: Shipyard Profile: Joey D'Isernia and Eastern Shipbuilding Group Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Greg Trauthwein , Editor Gregory R. Trauthwein has covered the global maritime market for more than 25... November 16, 2026 Eastern's Allanton shipyard, encompassing approximately 300 acres, of which 160 are developed. Image courtesy ESG Image courtesy ESG Image courtesy ESG With three shipbuilding facilities, 1,300 employees and a diversified orderbook extending into the next decade, Eastern Shipbuilding Group (ESG) is well positioned to benefit from renewed investment in America's maritime industrial base. CEO Joey D'Isernia discusses the company's growth, its commercial and government contracts, and why workforce development and fundamental changes in shipbuilding practices are essential to a sustainable industry revival. American shipbuilding has received more attention from Washington, DC, in the past two years than it has in the past few decades combined. The Trump administration has made rebuilding the nation's maritime industrial base a political imperative, driven by national security concerns, China's dominance of global shipbuilding and the need to expand and modernize the U.S. fleet: navy, government ships and commercial. For shipbuilders, the renewed attention is welcome, but turning that political narrative into shipbuilding contracts, infrastructure improvements and a larger skilled workforce will take considerably longer. But Joey D'Isernia, CEO of Eastern Shipbuilding Group (ESG) , sees substantial opportunity in the renewed emphasis on maritime manufacturing. As the company celebrates its 50th anniversary, he remains focused on the practical considerations of operating a shipyard: selecting the right projects, investing in people and equipment, managing production and delivering vessels. "There's a lot of really positive things that are out there," D'Isernia said of the federal initiatives. But much of the proposed legislation and announced funding is still moving through the system. "It's not going to have an overnight effect." Eastern, founded in 1976 and now led by the second generation of the D'Isernia family, operates three facilities across two counties in Northwest Florida. The privately held company employs approximately 1,300 people and serves commercial and government customers. D'Isernia describes Eastern as one of a relatively small number of remaining mid-tier American shipbuilders, with the engineering capability and physical infrastructure to handle a broad range of sophisticated vessel construction projects. Fifty Years of Investment Eastern's facilities include its Allanton shipyard , encompassing approximately 300 acres, of which 160 are developed; the 50-acre Nelson Street facility ; and its Port St. Joe yard . Each serves a distinct role in the company's operations, and each offers opportunities for future expansion. Over the years, Eastern has invested in larger launch ways and basins, additional crane capacity, fabrication facilities and other infrastructure improvements that have increased the size and complexity of vessels it can construct. As a privately held business, D'Isernia said Eastern has considerable flexibility to reinvest earnings in facilities, equipment and employees without the pressures that can accompany public ownership. Today, however, the investment priorities are changing. Rather than concentrating primarily on building larger vessels or increasing physical capacity, Eastern is emphasizing productivity improvements that allow its existing workforce to accomplish more. This includes additional covered fabrication space, process improvements and practical applications of automation. "We're heavily investing in covered fabrication area in levels of automation that are realistic for the U.S. shipbuilding industry," D'Isernia said. He cautions that technologies developed for large Asian shipyards do not necessarily translate directly to American commercial and government shipbuilding, where vessel designs, production volumes and customer requirements are substantially different. Eastern's approach is to invest in technologies that can improve efficiency without introducing unnecessary risk or creating new production problems. "When that thing came out, we just looked at it and said, we're the shipyard to build it." Joey D'Isernia, CEO, Eastern Shipbuilding Group , on the contract to build a trip of hybrid electric ferries for Washington State Ferries. A Diversified Orderbook Eastern's current construction program reflects the company's broad capabilities across commercial and government markets. At Allenton, Eastern is building four 84-foot harbor tugs for Saltchuk. The first two are approaching delivery, with the remaining vessels expected to follow within months. The yard is also building a 6,500-cubic-yard hopper dredge for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, with launch anticipated in spring 2027 and delivery targeted toward the end of that year. Following it through production is a 10,000-cubic-yard hopper dredge for The Dutra Group, representing a substantial investment in fleet renewal for the West Coast dredging contractor. Both dredges involve collaboration with Dutch dredging specialist Royal IHC. At Port St. Joe, Eastern is completing two 360-foot multipurpose subsea construction vessels for Hornbeck Offshore Services. Originally started at another shipyard, the projects were interrupted when that builder failed, leaving the vessels in litigation for approximately a decade. Taking over the projects required Eastern to assess partially completed construction, identify deficiencies, replace unusable materials and develop a path to completion. Eastern has developed experience in recovering troubled shipbuilding projects, a capability that D'Isernia believes distinguishes the company. The mix of tugs, dredges, offshore vessels, ferries and naval construction also reflects a deliberate strategy of diversification. "There's no ideal mix," D'Isernia said of balancing commercial and government work. "We want to take on the right risks. We want to match our expertise and our core competencies to the right projects." That approach provides flexibility as market conditions and federal procurement priorities change. Image courtesy ESG A Big Win: Washington State Ferries One of Eastern's most important recent contracts is its selection to build three hybrid electric ferries for Washington State Ferries (WSF). The approximately 400-foot vessels represent a major addition to Eastern's commercial orderbook and build on its experience constructing large passenger ferries, including the three Staten Island ferries delivered previously. The initial Washington contract was valued at approximately $714 million for two vessels. Eastern subsequently received the option award for a third ferry, extending the program's importance to the yard. For D'Isernia, the opportunity was significant because Washington had historically restricted ferry construction to shipyards within the state. Legislative changes opened the competition to other American builders. "When that thing came out, we just looked at it and said, we're the shipyard to build it," he said. The ferries feature hybrid electric propulsion and are designed to complete their operating missions entirely on battery power.D'Isernia believes the project is particularly well-suited to Eastern's engineering capabilities. The company currently employs approximately 70 to 80 engineers, and electrical engineering is among its strongest disciplines. "Our electrical design team is top-notch, and this particular vessel with the hybrid electric design was just a great opportunity for us to showcase those capabilities," he said. D'Isernia also credited Washington State Ferries for investing heavily in design development before construction, particularly through its work with ABB. That preparation allowed Eastern to focus on optimizing equipment arrangements, accessibility, maintainability and production efficiency rather than resolving fundamental engineering questions after steel cutting. The state exercised its option for the third ferry as construction began on the first vessel, a decision D'Isernia views as validation of the yard's performance during design development. The program extends Eastern's Allanton workload through 2032 and could lead to additional opportunities as Washington continues replacing aging vessels. "We want to build more," D'Isernia said. "They need more. They need a steady pipeline of recapitalization, and we want to be their shipyard of choice to build out that fleet." Image courtesy ESG Eastern Shipbuilding Group is Building for the Navy Eastern is also participating in naval construction through its partnership with HII's Ingalls Shipbuilding division -- an example of distributed shipbuilding where naval shipbuilders use qualified partner yards to manufacture substantial vessel sections. At Nelson Street, the company is producing fully outfitted structural units for the U.S. Navy's Arleigh Burke class guided missile destroyers. Eastern has delivered a major block for DDG 135, is completing another for DDG 137 and has received an additional award for a subsequent destroyer. The yard is also producing outfitted units for HII's San Antonio class amphibious transport docks (LPD). D'Isernia estimates that distributed construction currently accounts for approximately 10% or less of Eastern's orderbook, although the company has capacity and interest in expanding that business. He emphasizes that successful distributed shipbuilding requires considerably more than fabrication capability. Large outfitted units involve thousands of components, extensive scheduling, supplier coordination, documentation and quality assurance. "We're really a force multiplier," D'Isernia said, explaining that Eastern helps HII manage material flow, identify problems and maintain production schedules. "It's one thing for somebody to send you stuff and send you drawings and you just put it in. It's another to schedule it, track it, do all the QA call-outs properly." Eastern sees additional potential in this model, provided it can balance subcontracted naval construction with its broader commercial and government workload. The 50-acre Nelson Street facility. Image courtesy ESG Rebuilding the Workforce Remains Job 1 Despite the attention given to robotics and advanced manufacturing, D'Isernia identifies skilled labor as the industry's most significant obstacle. "The number one constraint in U.S. shipbuilding today is a skilled workforce." He attributes the shortage to decades of declining participation in shipbuilding trades, a problem that cannot be resolved through short term recruitment campaigns alone. Eastern is addressing the challenge through competitive compensation, employee retention, educational partnerships, apprenticeship programs and on the job training. Its initiatives include a Maritime Training Academy in Gulf County and partnerships with high schools, vocational institutions and colleges. One particularly successful initiative involves high school welding students designing and fabricating artificial reefs that are subsequently deployed offshore. The program combines technical education with interests relevant to the surrounding coastal communities. Eastern also recruits inexperienced workers into general labor positions, allowing them to become familiar with shipyard operations before progressing into skilled trades. D'Isernia believes these programs are effective, but insufficient to address the national workforce shortage. He advocates substantially stronger federal incentives to attract workers into shipbuilding, potentially drawing on approaches used for military recruitment. Automation can reduce certain labor requirements, but he cautions against treating it as a comprehensive solution. "You can spool pipe and you can bend it on benders and you can have automated welding and all these things, but somebody has to install it in the ship." Lessons Learned D'Isernia sees opportunities for American shipyards to adopt production practices from South Korea, Japan and other leading shipbuilding nations, but believes an important structural difference must first be addressed. In major Asian commercial shipyards, builders generally exercise substantial control over vessel design, equipment selection and procurement. This enables standardized production, repeatable engineering and greater control over suppliers. In the United States, vessel owners and independent designers frequently determine equipment selections and design details, resulting in extensive customization. Even relatively minor equipment substitutions can affect machinery arrangements, electrical systems, cable routing and installation requirements. D'Isernia believes this limits the efficiencies available through automation and repetitive construction. "You can't just take the model of South Korea and dump it over here and expect it to work," he said. Greater shipbuilder control over design and supply chains, he believes, would improve productivity while creating more opportunities to apply advanced manufacturing technology. Eastern Shipbuilding Groups Port St. Joe yard. Image courtesy ESG Turning Policy Into Orders Looking ahead, D'Isernia believes the renewed federal commitment to shipbuilding must translate into economic incentives that encourage commercial operators to replace aging vessels and expand their fleets. Government shipbuilding can grow through increased appropriations and procurement. Commercial construction depends on vessel owners having sufficient financial justification to invest. He believes meaningful subsidies, tax incentives and depreciation benefits could help make fleet recapitalization economically viable, particularly for Jones Act operators. "Washington is going to have to take a bigger risk on shipbuilding," he said. Eastern sees potential across several commercial vessel sectors, although offshore oil and gas remains relatively quiet. D'Isernia noted that many offshore vessel operators continue to exercise financial discipline following the industry's downturn beginning in 2014, despite the advancing age of their fleets. Ultimately, he believes rebuilding American shipbuilding will require sustained investment, workforce development and procurement reform across multiple administrations. "Strengthening the shipbuilding industrial base is a national security and economic security priority," he said. "It's not a partisan thing." For Eastern, the immediate priorities remain executing its existing orderbook, improving productivity and maintaining the flexibility to respond as markets develop. The company's facilities may change considerably over the next five years, depending on demand and the types of vessels customers require. Its underlying business philosophy, D'Isernia maintains, will remain consistent. "We've been around for 50 years and we want to be here for at least 50 more years." As Eastern enters its second half century, the opportunity is substantial. Whether the broader American shipbuilding revival succeeds will depend less on the volume of political announcements than on sustained investment, a stronger workforce and the ability of shipyards to deliver vessels efficiently and consistently. End of a shift, workers punching out. Image courtesy ESG

articles.title: Learning from Maritime History: The Hanseatic League
articles.summary: I remember a quick reference to the Hanseatic League in my Dutch history classes, but I did not learn much more about it until I came across another reference in a university class in the United States. Since then, I often think about the Hanseatic…
articles.body: Learning from Maritime History: The Hanseatic League Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. Rik van Hemmen , Contributor Rik van Hemmen is the President of Martin & Ottaway... November 16, 2026 Illustration gemini by Rik van Hemmen I remember a quick reference to the Hanseatic League in my Dutch history classes, but I did not learn much more about it until I came across another reference in a university class in the United States. Since then, I often think about the Hanseatic League and what it means in today’s world. The early form of the Hanseatic League goes back to the 1100s and consisted of friendly trading relationships between towns and merchant communities around the Baltic and North Sea. They fished for herring along there shores but then it suddenly disappeared in the 1200’s and was rediscovered closer to the North Sea. The movement of herring stocks was long something of a mystery. More recent research suggests that changes in fish populations were influenced by a combination of overfishing and environmental and climatic factors, although the precise causes remain debated. Either way, it was an early lesson in the interaction between natural resources, climate, and human economic activity. The German and Baltic fisheries were now faced with a problem — and an opportunity. Herring was a desirable commodity because Christians ate fish on Fridays and during other religious fasts. While herring was relatively cheap, it spoiled quickly. Salting was the main method of preservation, and salt came from Lüneburg, some distance inland from Lübeck. Salt could be shipped more easily through Hamburg, which helped establish maritime trade routes connecting salt production, fishing communities, and commercial centers. The Hanseatic trading network eventually connected places such as Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bergen, Norway, where preserved fish and other commodities could be exchanged and shipped onward. Nothing terribly special there. Maritime trade routes like this had waxed and waned for millennia around the world. Venice was doing something similar at about the same time in the Mediterranean. But there were subtle differences. While Venice often played for dominance and control of trade, the northern trade developed more as a league approach: the Hanseatic League. Instead of a monopoly, the Hanseatic League more closely resembled a cartel or, more accurately, a trade alliance. There are many options in the development of maritime trade. One can simply go with the traditional — and often incorrectly characterized — Viking approach of uncooperative rape and pillage (zero-sum trade), all the way to fully cooperative maritime trade. From a game-theory point of view, this northern trade had many of the hallmarks of an iterated prisoner's dilemma. Instead of one big haul, the trade depended on long-term reliance and many transactions between partners, with each contributing a piece of the puzzle. That characteristic is extremely powerful and is a core source of cooperation in evolution, nature, social settings, and commerce. True maritime trade — not rape and pillage — needs credit, currency, contracts, and eventually financial agreements between financiers and the various cities and merchants involved in the trade. Next came insurance, trade agents, and other mechanisms for reducing commercial risk. Since it was a commercial venture, other cities and trading communities wanted in on the game. As long as everybody played by reasonably consistent rules, there was no obvious limit to its growth. Soon the trade expanded from fish to other products, and by the 1400s the Hanseatic League was a major force in northern European commerce, with trading connections extending from the eastern Baltic to London and along the Rhine to Cologne. Almost all the participants in the League were cities, and if one city stopped participating or violated the interests of the others, the other cities could boycott it or shift their trade, all without a formal central government structure. Meanwhile, very high levels of operational agreement and standardization strongly increased any merchant's holy grail: high predictability and steady profits. It was far from all sweets and roses. The cities also maintained military capabilities, and ships from different cities could be combined into fleets to fight aggressors and pirates. While nowhere near as glitzy as the Southern Renaissance, the Northern Renaissance was real and had its own character, although the distinction between a "Northern" and "Southern" Renaissance can be overstated. The differing commercial environments did, however, influence local philosophy and political thought. The North talked in terms of Erasmus—humanism and moral ethics—while the South talked in terms of Machiavelli—power and dominance. Crazily, Erasmus and Machiavelli were almost exact contemporaries, and the comparison of their philosophies can seem to describe today's political polarizations almost exactly. A maritime trade network can create great wealth, with inherently high incomes per person. This is difficult to achieve on land, where the transportation of trade goods was incredibly expensive and therefore constrained economic growth. However, feudal landed gentry had its own asset: serfs, and the ability to whip them up in envy of nearby Hanseatic towns. While a single sailor can carry many times more cargo than a serf, on land a serf with a gun is no worse than a sailor with a gun. This instability contributed to the demise of many city-states and the creation and consolidation of nation-states in both the South and North of Europe. The Hanseatic League eventually disappeared, but so did the great maritime republics of the Southern Renaissance. Venice lasted longer, in part because it took longer for nation-states to organize and challenge its position in the Mediterranean. In effect, neither model proved immune to the rise of the nation-state. This would indicate that the Northern and Southern Renaissance concepts were both doomed. But maybe not, and maybe the Northern approach holds more inherent promise. After a number of centuries of nation-state strife, what we have today is a Europe that, in some important respects, functions more like a Hanseatic League than a Venetian single-entity dominance model. Just like the Hanseatic League, in the European Union—and NATO—there are misguided efforts at freeloading, overplaying one's hand, and even moves to secede, along with lots of bickering. But as long as they stick together and work together, everybody in the league benefits. It would appear that the Northern Renaissance concept is the real winner and perhaps can be Ben Franklin paraphrased as: "It is a league, if you can keep it." REUTERS/Thomas Peter A Somali-flagged cargo ship carrying nearly 3,000 metric tons of wheat capsized off Bulgaria on Monday after what crew members described as an attack by two sea drones, marking the latest in a growing series of strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea. All 12 crew members aboard the BETUL 8 were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian military helicopters and naval vessels from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey. According to Bulgaria’s Ministry of Transport and Communications , the Maritime Rescue Coordination Center in Varna received a distress call at approximately 9:15 a.m. local time reporting that the vessel was sinking about 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra, within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The vessel was sailing from Tulcea, Romania, to Egypt with a cargo of bulk wheat. Bulgarian maritime news outlet Maritime.bg , which spoke with surviving crew members, reported that two unmanned surface vessels struck the ship before it capsized. The publication also obtained photographs from the crew purportedly showing the drones involved in the attack. Survivors separately described the attack to Bulgarian National Television . Bulgarian authorities have not publicly identified who was responsible for the reported attack, and the origin of the drones remains unconfirmed. The rescue operation involved four vessels from the multinational Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Group, along with two Bulgarian Air Force Cougar helicopters and an Su-25 aircraft deployed to survey the area. The helicopters reached the scene and evacuated the crew from life rafts using rescue baskets. All 12 seafarers were transported to Bulgaria’s Chaika Naval Helicopter Air Base. The Bulgarian Transport Ministry said the survivors were in generally good condition, although they were suffering from exposure to the cold. Bulgarian naval officials later reported that one crew member had sustained a minor cut to the head. An aerial survey confirmed that the vessel had overturned. Bulgarian naval officials said the ship was lying upside down, with part of its bow remaining above the water. A naval vessel was dispatched to assess potential marine pollution. There was no immediate confirmation of an oil spill or other environmental damage. The incident comes amid an escalating series of attacks on merchant vessels operating near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, raising concerns about the safety of commercial shipping routes in the western Black Sea. On Sunday, gCaptain reported that three commercial vessels had been struck by drones near Romania’s Sulina canal , a critical shipping corridor connecting the Danube River with the Black Sea. Romanian authorities reported no casualties in those attacks. The latest incident underscores the growing risks to merchant ships operating in waters bordering NATO members Romania and Bulgaria as the maritime consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war continue to spread. The cause of the BETUL 8 casualty and responsibility for the reported drone attack remain under investigation. articles.title: Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test
articles.summary: The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. articles.body: Greater China Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test Splash November 17, 2026 0 370 4 minutes read Zhejiang University Zhejiang University The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. The latest chapter from our brand new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Three sets of initials still define Hong Kong’s rise as a shipowning powerhouse: Y.K. Pao (pictured), C.Y. Tung and T.Y. Chao. Their generation transformed a trading entrepôt into one of the world’s great centres of private shipownership, building fleets across oceans and relationships across political divides. What they created was more than a collection of ships. It was a distinctive business culture: discreet, entrepreneurial, internationally connected and, despite the huge sums involved, keenly aware of financial risk and the danger of assuming that a freight boom will last forever. Its strength has always been an ability to think in decades while trading in markets that can turn in weeks. That instinct is hard earned, not evidence of perfect judgement. The debt crisis that engulfed Orient Overseas following C.Y. Tung’s death in 1982 is a reminder that even the city’s most celebrated shipowners have misread a cycle. Hong Kong’s commercial memory includes the failures as well as the fortunes. Now the question is whether those instincts can survive another transition: the transfer of control to generations with more ways than ever to invest their inheritance, and more places from which to run a shipping business. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association (HKSOA), describes owners who combine “global ambition with a healthy respect for cycles”. They have lived through recessions, SARS, the pandemic and repeated geopolitical shocks, he says, and learned to protect liquidity, limit leverage and stay close to their customers and ships. It is a substantial community. HKSOA members owned, managed or operated around 180m dwt at the end of 2025. Those figures are not a count of vessels directly owned by Hong Kong families, but they demonstrate the continuing heft of the wider owner-manager network. Hext also points to owners’ involvement in safety, decarbonisation and talent development. “Those are not the behaviours of a community that has lost interest in its industry,” he says. Nor has this decade been uniformly miserable for owners. Pandemic-era disruption brought extraordinary returns in some segments, while subsequent wars, rerouting, sanctions and trade tensions created both windfalls and frightening exposure. The successful Hong Kong response has generally been less about calling every market turn than ensuring a business can withstand the next one. Niraj Nanda, chief commercial officer at Anglo-Eastern, points to selective fleet renewal, disposals at attractive prices and the retention of cash. “In a cyclical business, the important discipline is to use the good years not only to grow, but also to prepare for the rainy day that will eventually come,” he says. That conservatism should not be confused with timidity. Wah Kwong Maritime Transport, founded by T.Y. Chao in 1952 and now led by the family’s third generation, has launched Wah Kwong Bulk with ambitions to operate 50 to 60 vessels by 2030. It has also ordered new LR2 tankers and moved into port electrification through its Wah Kwong NatPower venture. This is a traditional shipowning name extending its reach rather than retreating. Elsewhere, Valles Steamship remains in the hands of the Koo family, with a fourth generation involved in the business. The Tung family provides a more complicated illustration of continuity. It sold its flagship liner business, OOCL, to COSCO in 2018, but continues to operate in shipping through the much smaller, privately held Island Navigation. The scale changes; the maritime inheritance survives. The Banga family offers another contemporary succession story. Angad Banga succeeded his father Harry as chief executive of The Caravel Group this year, taking responsibility for a business spanning ships, shipmanagement, commodities and investments, including a significant shareholding in Pacific Basin. “For our family, shipping is not simply an asset class. It is an industry we believe in deeply,” Banga says. His emphasis is on stewardship rather than reinventing the business, and on leaving it stronger for those who follow. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, observes that several established families now have “third and fourth generations in the saddle”. But the picture is not universal. Some heirs regard shipping as a vocation; others see one investment among many. Bjorn Hojgaard, chief executive of Anglo-Eastern, is candid about the change. “The picture is mixed, and it would be unfair to generalise,” he says. Families increasingly manage wealth through professional structures, allocating money across property, private credit, technology and other investments. For some, shipping becomes one component of a diversified portfolio rather than the organising purpose of the family business. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, puts the succession challenge sharply: “Shipping therefore has to compete for family capital rather than assume it will inherit it.” More importantly, he argues, the next generation must be able to build a modern shipping enterprise in Hong Kong, not simply administer ships acquired by their parents or grandparents. That brings the debate beyond family loyalty to the city’s competitiveness. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, identifies “domicile drift” as a particular danger: internationally educated, mobile heirs can put family offices, investment mandates and commercial decisions wherever regulation, costs and opportunities suit them best. Recent events show how quickly that can happen. Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin moved strategic leadership and commercial decision-making to Singapore in 2025 amid US-China port-fee tensions, while Seaspan also relocated its headquarters to the city-state. The subsequent suspension of those fees does not undo the lesson: the location of a vessel’s flag, its ownership company and the people making decisions can change with remarkable speed. The threat, therefore, is not an imminent extinction of Hong Kong’s shipping families. It is a gradual thinning out of the city’s decision-making ecosystem. If the next generation continues to own vessels but chooses to finance, charter and direct them elsewhere, Hong Kong can retain impressive maritime statistics while losing some of the commercial influence that made those statistics possible. Survival, though, is not quite the same as renewal. Hong Kong needs new principals willing to build companies, not only heirs prepared to preserve existing ones. The survival of this unique breed ultimately depends on more than inherited loyalty. The city must remain somewhere a young owner wants to take risk, build relationships, hire talent and commit capital. The names on the office doors may be familiar, but the business behind them cannot stand still. To access the full magazine for free, click here .
