articles.body: Contributions Finance and Insurance Operations The East India company without a charter Splash November 17, 2026 0 194 6 minutes read Carriers and port groups are rebuilding the oldest form of trade finance – financing the cargo they carry. Sergey Belskiy follows the money from Venice to DP World and asks who pays. In July 2025, DP World reported that its finance arm had financed more than $1 billion of trade. Behind it stand 32 financial institutions, among them J.P. Morgan, which has shared risk with a port operator since June 2025. By December, the Asian Development Bank was still putting the trade finance gap at $2.5 trillion, with 41% of applications from small and medium-sized enterprises refused. The bank that turns a client away at its own counter is financing him through the owner of the terminal. Trade finance is passing from banks to the owners of the cargo flow – shipping lines, port and logistics groups, and their trading subsidiaries. Not because the banks have run out of money. And the cargo owner will pay for the move in something other than interest. What the bank is short of Capital has not left trade finance: at the top it is in surplus, and the shortage is of bankable structure. Two things decide what follows. Holding a short trade asset on a bank balance sheet has become expensive, so the money is accumulating elsewhere. And checking a mid-market file costs a bank more than the fee earns, because knowledge of the goods sits with whoever sails the ship, runs the terminal and issues the bill of lading, for whom the counterparty check is a by-product of the booking. Hence the rule that governs this market’s whole history: trade is financed by whoever holds the mobile capital of the day, and knowledge of the goods decides only through whose hands that capital reaches the cargo. Goods, carriage and money have twice come together in one pair of hands and twice come apart. DP World is the third time, and the order of that alternation says how large it will be – and who will pay. The spiral Venice from the eleventh to the fourteenth century financed trade voyage by voyage. Money was not scarce, but there was no instrument to keep it: the sea loan and later the colleganza gathered it into a single voyage – a doge held half his fortune in such contracts – and dissolved on the ship’s return. One contract, one voyage – that was the ceiling. What changed in Genoa was the form of the claim. The commune, at war almost without pause, borrowed from its own citizens and cut the debt into shares that transferred by a simple ledger entry. For the first time capital could be held and passed on without entering any venture. Trade finance went to the class that lived on those claims – the banking house, lending at interest. From that day the merchant, risking nothing himself, pays those who go to sea. Genoa had fortresses, a transferable share and durable institutions – the Maona of Chios lasted until 1566 – but not broad accumulation: its shareholders were the commune’s own creditors, the same closed circle. The East India companies became possible where accumulation broke out of that circle. The 1602 subscription of the Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC) raised about 6.4 million guilders, and in the Amsterdam chamber alone 1,143 people subscribed, a maidservant among them. Only one form gathers a mass like that: joint-stock capital locked in for ten years – in practice never returned – with a share the investor could not redeem, only sell on. The VOC produced the exchange, not the reverse. Its charter gave it a monopoly too, and the shipper got one buyer where he had had a market. The nineteenth century pulled everything apart again, and again capital decided it. The industrial revolution gathered the short-term part of its surplus into the deposits of joint-stock banks. The London deposit bank lent thousands of other people’s balances, so trade was financed by the custodian of capital rather than its owner, at a price no private fortune could match. By 1913 roughly half of world trade ran on sterling bills drawn on London. Steam, the Suez Canal and the telegraph merely let that capital reach goods it never saw. Every time financing left the cargo flow, it built an instrument that had not existed before: Genoa made the claim transferable, the nineteenth century built the deposit bank, the money market and negotiable title. Every time it returned, it returned holding that instrument, and so at a larger scale. Venice joined goods, carriage and money within a voyage. The East India companies joined them within a firm that outlived its founders, on the Genoese share, and this time they are being joined across a network, on everything the banks built: their money market funds it, their negotiable title has gone electronic. Two conclusions follow. First, the cargo owner won exactly once – when the function went to a bank that owned neither ship nor goods, and money was cheaper than ever. He lost every time financing passed to someone who also had the disposal of his cargo. Second, this convergence will exceed the last one by as much as the banking instrument exceeds the Genoese share. Why now Capital has moved again. Money looking for yield is going past the banks, and the carriers have capital of their own: the container lines’ combined net profit over 2021 and 2022 came to some $364 billion, after twelve years in which the industry’s cumulative bottom line was negative. Knowledge of the goods, a public good for a century and a half, has become private again – it now sits inside the carrier’s system – and title is following. Since September 2023 the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act has given the electronic bill of lading the force of paper, and the FIT Alliance’s October survey puts adoption at 51.1%, with only 22.2% of banks reporting any use at all. The same order explains the earlier failures. Maersk piloted lending to shippers in India in 2016, and the product stayed niche for close to a decade: nothing scalable can be built on a paper bill of lading that travels by courier. TradeLens, the neutral platform Maersk built with IBM, closed in 2023 for want of the industry-wide collaboration it depended on. A platform has no cargo flow of its own. The exception is the Japanese sogo shosha, which never separated trading, carriage and finance. Berkshire Hathaway began buying into all five of them in 2019 and by September 2026 held more than 10% of each, a ceiling it had promised never to cross and the houses agreed to lift, with a stated horizon of fifty years or forever. The most conservative capital in the world saw the form before the market had a name for it. The form is a buy-back, not a loan Credit is transitional. The flow owner’s logic leads to a buy-back. The group’s trading subsidiary buys the goods from the client, carries them on the group’s ships under its own electronic bill of lading, and sells them back to the client, or to a buyer the client names, at the discharge port, on deferred terms and at a price that includes the cost of money. In law it is a sale. In economics it is financing secured on the goods themselves, with title held by the financing party throughout. The agreed repurchase closes the price risk, and where it fails the cargo goes to another buyer in the group’s network. The borrower’s credit risk becomes resale risk, which is what a global carrier carries better than a bank: a bank can take title too, but it cannot sell the cargo on. A company that buys and sells goods is not a bank, and bank capital requirements do not reach it. What is left for the banks is the wholesale money – the J.P. Morgan arrangement with DP World is the prototype. Are we heading for new East India companies? Yes, but not the ones people expect. No charters, no garrisons, no flag: what is being rebuilt is the commercial core – one counterparty owning the ship, the terminal, title to the cargo and the money advanced against it. The monopoly comes not from an exclusive right but from the bundle: every line in it is competitive on its own – freight, storage, finance – but they are quoted as one number. The structure has three limits, and two work by themselves: the groups compete, and supervision is already looking this way – the US Federal Maritime Commission counted some $15.4 billion of demurrage and detention collected by nine carriers over five years. The third has to be built into the transaction: someone on the cargo owner’s side alone, who takes the bundle apart and puts an alternative against each line of that one number. An honest boundary: the flow owner will finance what he carries and can see, and that will not close $2.5 trillion. Capital is waiting for a structure it can buy. It is now clear who will present it and what it stands on: the instrument the banks spent a century and a half building. What remains open is whether the cargo owner walks into it with an alternative in hand. For a century and a half he could afford not to think about that: the money came from someone with no use for his cargo. That period is ending. November 16, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zulfugar Karimov Oil prices fell more than 1% on Monday as signs of recovering oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz reinforced expectations of surplus supply, though fresh tanker incidents underscored risks to Middle East exports. Brent crude futures were down $1.67, or 1.74%, at $94.17 a barrel by 1410 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude dropped $1.14, or 1.29%, to $87.42. The global oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping . "For the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, traders are actively contemplating the possibility of excess supply rather than persistent tightness," said KCM Trade's chief market analyst, Tim Waterer. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day (bpd) in the fourth quarter, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand, the IEA said. The agency had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. The IEA also gave more details of remaining volumes from a record release of oil reserves pledged by its members in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February, including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. About 15 million bpd of crude oil moved through the Strait of Hormuz in 2025, IEA data shows. Middle East supply and oil demand have adapted remarkably well to heightened shipping risks and higher prices, Goldman Sachs said in a note on Sunday. Goldman said it expects Brent to average $88 a barrel in 2027 and ease to $78 by the end of 2027 because of a return to surplus supply. Signs of lower demand in China, the world's second-largest oil consumer, also pressured prices. The latest data from the country's National Bureau of Statistics on Monday showed refinery throughput for October fell 2% from a month earlier and was down 8.1% from a year ago. The drop in throughput, along with an increase in domestic output and overseas imports, indicated a build in Chinese crude inventories of 492,000 bpd last month, according to Reuters calculations based on government data. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday that two oil tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz leading to explosions. Six tankers caught fire in similar incidents on Sunday and Monday, the Revolutionary Guards' statement added. Reuters could not independently verify the report. The recovery of oil export flows from producer group OPEC+ remains fragile, with regional supply still vulnerable to fresh disruptions, BMI analysts said in a client note. "As such, physical constraints on production and exports, alongside fluctuations in the geopolitical risk premium, will continue to dominate price action until a settlement is reached between Washington and Tehran." (Reuters)

And yet there’s more than enough crude on the global market. Saudi Arabia, the de facto leader of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, said it pumped 10.5 million barrels a day in October, a level reached only once since 2022. Iraq and Kuwait also reported big increases, while the United Arab Emirates is now free of OPEC quotas, allowing it to pump as much as it wants. Gulf shipments nudged lower this week, but remain healthy despite a slew of attacks, according to TankerTrackers.com Inc. The ample supply has added to pressure on oil prices. Futures at one point this week were down almost 25% for the month, easing inflation concerns and offering respite for the global economy. Prices for physical cargoes have also plummeted, as producers compete for customers and exorbitant shipping costs begin to thaw. The recovery is still precarious. Attacks have killed at least one seafarer this month and spilled oil is washing ashore on the region’s beaches. With shipping under constant threat and Iranian media claiming attacks on navigational equipment near Hormuz, oil flows are erratic and could slow at any moment. But Emirati officials at a recent conference in Abu Dhabi were keen to stress the resilience of the industry. That ability to keep crude flowing, mirrored across the Gulf, has helped bring Middle East shipments back toward pre-war levels and pushed Brent crude prices below $90 a barrel at one point this week. “For us national shipping companies, there is no choice,” Khalid Alhammad, president of ship management for Saudi vessel owner Bahri, said at a conference in Dubai. “We still have to go through the Strait of Hormuz. We have to keep moving the energy.” It’s a remarkable turnaround from some of the worst fears at the outset of the war. Before the conflict, about a fifth of the world’s oil flowed through Hormuz, and analysts warned that a closure could send crude prices above $200 a barrel. Last week at Adipec, the Middle East’s biggest oil conference, senior executives agreed that crude markets look well supplied heading into 2027, with further price declines potentially easing the fight against inflation, though efforts to rebuild stockpiles depleted during the war could limit how far they fall. The recovery reached a milestone Friday, when the International Energy Agency said oil supply was outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. Rising production beyond the Gulf has helped cushion global markets, with weekly US crude output topping 14 million barrels a day for the first time and the latest figures from Brazil and Guyana all at records. The IEA said the shift, alongside a plunge in physical crude prices, suggested the market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing.” Pockets of tightness persist. Fuel prices remain far higher than crude, with European diesel trading at about $170 a barrel, for example. Shipping costs are also still historically elevated. Transporting crude from the US to Asia adds roughly 20% to the price of American oil, more than double the premium a year ago. Yet even those strains have eased. Freight markets remain elevated, but are well below the extremes seen a month ago. US retail gasoline prices have also fallen below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association. “The return of supply from the Gulf has depressed prices, coupled with the deflation of the freight bubble,” said Sasha Foss, an analyst at Marex Group’s CSC Commodities. “The market is less stressed than it was, but October was the biggest month for vessel incidents in Hormuz, so there are still risks.” The rebalancing has come at a cost. Vitol Group, the world’s top independent oil trader, said recently that the Iran war has cut global oil consumption by about 3 million barrels a day, an assessment echoed by other major traders. The market, in other words, is finding its footing partly because the war has sharply curtailed demand across fuels and regions. China’s crude imports fell about 15% from a year earlier to 9.9 million barrels a day in October. European nations have reported double-digit declines in diesel demand, while US gasoline consumption was marginally lower than a year earlier during the peak summer driving season. The supply recovery began in earnest over the summer and has gathered pace since then. It shows up in a steady uptick in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, as traders unload cargoes onto new ships just outside Hormuz as part of a burgeoning shuttle trade. It has left traders with plenty of cargoes to sell. This week, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. slashed the price of its flagship crude grade to attract buyers. Saudi Arabia also cut its key oil prices, though the kingdom is selling fewer barrels under long-term contracts than before the war, making its pricing harder to track. Instead, it has increasingly turned to ad hoc sales. The cuts underscore just how much oil is leaving the Gulf, even as tankers remain under attack. “The workarounds and the shuttle system have managed to keep these prices from going sky-high,” said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital. “There’s a question of durability. We’ve gone through a period where the Iranians didn’t cause much havoc in the Strait. But lately, that’s ramped up again, and there’s a concern that this could go off the rails.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Avigator Fortuner/Shutterstock The gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal is expected to release vessel capacity absorbed by lengthy diversions around Africa, but persistent port congestion and major network adjustments could keep supply chains under pressure well into 2027, according to DHL Global Forwarding. In a market assessment published Monday , DHL said more than 10% of the global container shipping fleet remains tied up in port congestion, representing approximately 3.6 million TEU of capacity. The bottlenecks persist even as carriers begin restoring services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Around 60% of relevant Asia-Europe headhaul services are currently planned to operate through Suez, although the return remains uneven across trade lanes, DHL said. The transition could take another six to 12 months as carriers reposition vessels, rebalance schedules and adjust networks that have spent years operating around the Cape of Good Hope. That timeline assumes security conditions do not force further changes. The assessment comes as Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced additional structural changes to their Gemini Cooperation services through the Suez Canal, marking another step toward restoring traditional Asia-Europe shipping routes. While shorter voyages free up vessels previously committed to longer routes, DHL warned that the additional capacity will not necessarily translate into reliable schedules. “Carriers must reposition ships, rebalance schedules and manage services operating across different routings,” said Bjoern Schoon, Senior Vice President of Ocean Freight at DHL Global Forwarding Asia Pacific. The changes are unfolding as the global containership fleet continues to expand. DHL’s November Ocean Freight Market Update forecasts fleet capacity growth of approximately 4% in 2026, while global ocean freight demand has increased 5% year to date. Meanwhile, DHL cited Linerlytica data showing that containership orders reached 6.4 million TEU so far this year, bringing the orderbook to approximately 47.8% of the active fleet. The combination of new ships, shorter Suez voyages and ongoing port congestion is creating increasingly uneven market conditions. DHL said freight rates are showing signs of weakness on some Asia-Europe services, while the transpacific market remains comparatively firm. In the Middle East, strong demand and severe congestion continue to support higher rates, with berth delays exceeding two weeks at some Gulf gateways. For shippers, the result is a market where additional fleet capacity does not necessarily mean faster or more dependable cargo movements. The logistics company expects schedule reliability, rather than available capacity alone, to remain a key challenge as shipping networks adjust through 2027. articles.body: Environment Europe Operations Regulatory Greek shipowners put Brussels on the spot over IMO deadlock Adis Ajdin November 17, 2026 0 710 1 minute read UGS UGS Greek shipowners have launched a fresh attack on Brussels ahead of the next round of international shipping emissions negotiations, accusing the European Union of putting its own regulatory interests ahead of a global agreement. Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlos warned on Monday that the EU’s unwillingness to compromise risks pushing the International Maritime Organization into another deadlock when talks resume in London next week. Travlos said there had been no meaningful progress since the previous negotiating round in September and questioned whether Brussels was more interested in preserving its regional carbon regulations and the revenue they generate than securing a worldwide deal. Greece and three other EU member states, together controlling around 70% of Europe’s shipping fleet according to Travlos, have repeatedly called for greater flexibility in the European negotiating position. Those appeals, she said, had gone unanswered. The intervention comes ahead of a November 23–27 IMO working group meeting, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee’s 85th session from November 30 to December 3. A further extraordinary session has been scheduled provisionally for December 4, subject to confirmation. The talks will revisit the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, which combines a global marine fuel standard with an emissions-pricing mechanism. The negotiations have been held up by disagreements over the design, cost and implementation of the measures. Travlos called for a framework reflecting the availability and cost of alternative fuels, the readiness of supporting infrastructure and competition for new fuels from other industries. She also argued that energy-efficiency improvements and operational measures must remain part of the emissions-reduction toolkit rather than placing almost all the emphasis on alternative fuels. Greek owners have long favoured a single international regulatory regime over overlapping regional requirements. The latest statement sharpens that position by directly questioning the EU’s negotiating intentions just days before governments return to London. articles.title: The Future of Maritime Safety: Navigating the Polar Frontier’s Uncharted Waters and Hidden Hazards
articles.summary: The Arctic and Antarctic are increasingly becoming areas of convergence for maritime industries and government operations. Commercial shipping, offshore energy, expedition cruising, recreational yachting, scientific research, coast guard, and naval...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The Arctic and Antarctic are increasingly becoming areas of convergence for maritime industries and government operations. Commercial shipping, offshore energy, expedition cruising, recreational yachting, scientific research, coast guard, and naval operations are all placing greater attention on these remote regions. For some, polar waters offer access to untapped natural resources and emerging shipping routes. For others, they provide opportunities for exploration, scientific discovery, and strategic operations in areas of growing geopolitical importance. But operating in these environments presents a unique set of challenges. Extreme weather, floating ice, limited infrastructure, and vast distances from support resources compound the risks associated with maritime operations. Even routine navigational decisions can carry significantly greater consequences when rescue capabilities and emergency response resources are hours or days away. Furthermore, the environmental sensitivity of these regions means that groundings, collisions, and pollution incidents can have lasting consequences. Understanding the environment above and below the waterline is critical to navigating these unforgiving waters. While radar, electronic charts, and other conventional navigation systems remain essential tools, they cannot always provide a complete picture of the hazards that lie ahead. In regions where chart data is sparse, satellite positioning can be degraded, and submerged hazards remain hidden from view, real-time underwater perception becomes an important part of safe vessel operations. For 25 years, FarSounder has developed technology to help mariners better understand their surroundings and navigate with greater confidence. Today, FarSounder’s Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonars are deployed on vessels operating in polar environments, including expedition cruise ships, polar research vessels, and naval platforms, some of which are icebreakers. These vessels leverage real-time awareness of the underwater environment to safely navigate some of the most remote and challenging waters on Earth. Navigating in Polar Regions Polar operations introduce unique hazards that complicate even the most routine maritime activities. Floating ice presents a significant navigational risk, as the visible portion above the surface may not accurately represent the size and shape of submerged ice keels below the waterline. Icebergs and other large ice masses can extend considerable distances beneath the surface, creating hazards that are difficult to assess through visual observation alone. The seafloor presents another challenge. In these regions, accurate chart data is sparse or nonexistent, leaving shallow bottoms, rocky pinnacles, and other underwater obstructions hidden. Even where charts are available, the underlying survey data may be outdated or lack the resolution necessary for safe navigation in unfamiliar waters. Navigation is further complicated by harsh weather conditions. High-latitude environments and magnetic anomalies can degrade the reliability of GPS and other positioning systems. Satellite communications may be intermittent, limiting a vessel’s ability to access external information or maintain consistent connectivity with shore-based resources. Extreme weather, fog, precipitation, and frigid temperatures can reduce the effectiveness of radar and optical sensors, making it more difficult to identify hazards above the surface. These challenges are amplified by the isolation of polar operations. Search and rescue efforts in these regions face extreme logistical difficulties, complicating both the detection of vessels in distress and the ability to safely reach them. An incident that might be relatively manageable in more populated waters can quickly become a serious emergency when support is far beyond reach. Groundings and collisions also present an increased risk to the surrounding environment. Oil spills and other pollution incidents are particularly difficult to contain in polar waters due to harsh operating conditions, limited infrastructure, and restricted response capabilities. These regions are also home to numerous native and migratory whale species, many of which are endangered. Vessel strikes remain a significant human-caused threat to whales, further elevating the environmental consequences of maritime operations. Underwater Perception Solution For 25 years, FarSounder has developed Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonar systems designed to provide real-time situational awareness of what lies beneath the surface ahead of the vessel. Argos sonars provide a real-time 3D image of the water column and seafloor out to distances of up to 1000 meters, enabling operators to make informed decisions before hazards become immediate threats. The Argos system’s low-frequency operation ensures that acoustic output remains benign to marine life, while still enabling the detection of large marine mammals such as whales. Ice, in particular, is an ideal sonar target. Its dense, reflective structure produces strong acoustic returns, allowing Argos systems to detect submerged ice masses that lie beneath the surface. At the same time, it maps the seafloor ahead at ranges of at least eight times the water depth below the sensor. In poorly charted or uncharted waters, this capability reveals shallows and obstructions like rocky pinnacles extending from the seafloor and moving hazards in the water column, including whales. In environments where GPS is degraded, communications are intermittent, and charts are unreliable, Argos systems continue to deliver consistent, real-time data. With a rapid update rate and the ability to scan from the seafloor to the surface in a single ping, operators gain a continuous understanding of the space ahead Polar Charts: Unreliable, Outdated, or Non-Existent Beyond underwater perception ahead, Argos sonars also create a map of the collected seafloor data. These recorded depth measurements are recalled when returning to a previous location, allowing vessels to identify and follow safe routes where chart data is unreliable. The sonar’s software enables this data to be anonymously shared across the FarSounder fleet . In return, vessels will gain access to an aggregate map of all other customer contributions. This program also supports global ocean mapping initiatives like Seabed 2030 . These crowdsourcing efforts have been able to provide tangible value for the broader maritime community operating in Arctic regions. FarSounder’s crowdsourced bathymetry (CSB) data is unique compared to most other CSB contributions in that it has high quality meta-data. This makes FarSounder customer CSB valuable in that it can be more reliably used for other applications. For example, because of the meta-data quality, CSB contributed by one of our customers transiting the Northwest Passage was included in an official chart produced by the Canadian Hydrographic Service. While poorly charted waters are an obvious concern for polar operators, the reliability of nautical charts is not exclusively an issue in remote regions. Even areas generally considered to be among the best surveyed and charted in the world can contain significant discrepancies between charted depths and actual seafloor conditions. Work conducted by Anthony Klemm, Physical Scientist at NOAA’s Coast Survey Development Lab, comparing crowdsourced bathymetry and satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) with NOAA’s BlueTopo database and official nautical charts, has identified numerous locations where charted depths differ dramatically from measured conditions. One example involved a FarSounder customer transiting off the coast of Massachusetts near Nantucket. During the voyage, the vessel passed over a shoal charted to be approximately 10–12 meters deep. However, measurements collected by the vessel’s Argos sonar indicated that the actual depth was closer to 5 meters. The measured data was shared through the IHO Data Centre for Digital Bathymetry (DCDB). Anthony analyzed the contribution and found that the shoal identified in the crowdsourced data correlated with a seafloor trend visible in satellite-derived bathymetry for the same location. Fortunately, the transiting vessel was a relatively shallow-draft pleasure craft. However, had a larger commercial vessel passed over the same shoal, particularly at low tide, the discrepancy could have resulted in a grounding. This example is not an isolated occurrence. Using crowdsourced bathymetry data, Anthony has been developing automated tools to identify additional locations where charted depths may not accurately reflect actual conditions, including waters generally considered to be among the best charted areas in the world. These findings highlight an important consideration for maritime operators: even official nautical charts cannot always be relied upon to provide a complete representation of the underwater environment. In remote polar regions, where hydrographic survey coverage is significantly limited, the potential for encountering unknown hazards is even greater. Improving Awareness in the World’s Most Remote Waters For FarSounder, these challenges are not simply theoretical. Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonars have been installed on ice-classed hulls, icebreakers, and customer vessels that regularly operate in polar regions for more than two decades. Expedition cruise ships and explorer yachts leverage this technology to reach remote destinations, providing truly unique experiences for guests onboard. Icebreakers, naval ships, and research vessels are able to identify submerged ice and underwater obstacles, helping to reduce risk and extend operations into locations critical to their missions. Customers have experienced firsthand the difference that real-time underwater awareness can make in these environments. Ice Pilot Captain Clive Shute described his first experience using Argos while navigating ice-rich waters off Greenland: “I was lucky to have the opportunity to use FarSounder’s Argos Forward Looking Sonar for the first time recently. We were taking the ship in the ice-rich waters off Greenland. Having the Argos system installed proved to be a game-changer in safety.” Other customers have shared examples of Argos identifying hazards that conventional navigation tools failed to reveal. Captain Walter Wetmore described an instance where the system identified a shoreline that was incorrectly represented on the chart, helping the vessel avoid a potential grounding and avoid floating ice while navigating fjords: “The system clearly showed a shoreline, which was incorrectly shown on the chart, and helped avoid a grounding. It also showed growlers and bergy bits when traveling up the fjords. I will not travel to areas of ice again without the FarSounder systems.” For some operators, the technology has become an essential part of their ability to undertake these voyages in the first place. Reflecting on the capabilities Argos sonars provides while exploring remote polar waters, the owner of MY Warbird offered a simple but powerful statement: “We would not have gone that far north without the FarSounder.” As more sectors of the maritime industry shift their focus toward polar regions, the need for reliable, real-time underwater perception will continue to grow. FarSounder’s technology provides an innovative solution backed by 25 years of experience supporting those operating in some of the world’s most challenging maritime environments. articles.summary: The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity...

Photo courtesy DP World The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030. The Department for Transport’s proposal , published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data. The proposed framework would regulate all energy used on domestic voyages between UK ports, 50% of energy used on international voyages to and from the UK, and energy consumed by covered ships while at berth in British ports. Rather than mandating particular fuels, the regulation would establish progressively tightening limits on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of energy consumed by ships. Operators could meet those requirements through alternative fuels, electrification and other lower-emission energy sources. The government is also considering compliance flexibility mechanisms, including pooling, banking and borrowing emissions credits, similar to provisions under FuelEU Maritime. However, several important details remain undecided, including how quickly emissions limits would tighten and whether the UK should follow the EU’s trajectory, align with future IMO standards or establish its own targets. The government expects the regulation to take effect from 2030. The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies. “We welcome the Government moving forward with this consultation. Greater long-term certainty can help unlock the investment needed to decarbonise shipping, but regulation needs to develop alongside the fuels, infrastructure and technology that operators will need,” a Chamber spokesperson said. “Any future UK framework must be practical, support investment and maintain the international competitiveness of UK shipping.” The Chamber has previously called for a regulatory framework that avoids duplicating existing international requirements while providing operators with sufficient flexibility to manage the transition. In an October policy paper, the organization recommended aligning fuel certification and lifecycle emissions accounting with emerging IMO standards, developing reliable monitoring and verification systems, and setting targets based on realistic assessments of fuel availability and infrastructure readiness. Those concerns are particularly relevant given the significant overlap between ships trading to the UK and those already subject to European regulations. According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports. The consultation comes as the international shipping industry continues to grapple with uncertainty surrounding the IMO’s proposed global Net-Zero Framework. While the UK government acknowledges that international regulation remains the most effective way to reduce shipping emissions, it argues that uncertainty over global measures should not prevent domestic action. The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026. The government is also seeking industry feedback on whether smaller ships should eventually be included, with vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage remaining under review. Beyond the emissions requirements themselves, the consultation examines the availability of alternative maritime fuels, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness and the investment needed to support widespread adoption. The Department for Transport has emphasized that its proposals are preliminary and that no final regulatory decisions have been made. The consultation remains open until February 22, 2027 . The UK Chamber of Shipping said it will work with its members and the UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition to develop a detailed response addressing the operational, commercial and technical implications of the proposed framework. articles.title: Supertanker Rates Plunge More Than 60% From Record Highs
articles.summary: The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche LONDON, Nov 16 (Reuters) – The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October. Freight ?rates for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying ?oil from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 308 ?on the Worldscale basis on November 13, down by 64% from their record high of 841 on October 8, Baltic Exchange data shows. The plunge in rates came as Gulf oil exporters increased crude flows towards levels seen before the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The increase in flows has been achieved using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers and so-called dark crossings, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade detection, even as attacks against ships continued. The rise in Gulf oil exports reduced demand for crude shipped from other regions, freeing up VLCCs. “Gulf oil exports recently recovered to near prewar volumes, reducing Asian buyer demand for US and North Sea crudes, which in turn weighed on demand for tankers,” said Arrow Shipbroking analyst Delia He. Vortexa analyst Ioannis Papadimitriou said the recent spike in freight rates had reduced Asian demand for longer-haul US, West African and North Sea crude, which in turn increased the region’s use of Middle East crude, and that VLCC demand for longer voyages dropped as a result. “At the same time, vessel availability is building as ships discharge in East Asia,” he said. “As more tonnage is freed up, rates come under downward pressure.” EASING GEOPOLITICAL RISK PREMIUM Rates fell even more sharply on other routes, such as from West Africa to Asia. The jump in freight costs had been partly driven by factors including the perception of a higher risk of operating in the Middle East Gulf as Iran and the US attacked tankers, which had also pushed up oil prices. ExxonMobil Guyana has confirmed the first oil from Uaru , its fifth development in the Stabroek block, lifting the country’s installed production capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day, as the FPSO Errea Wittu joins the Destiny , Unity , Prosperity , and One Guyana units. In just over a decade, Guyana has become one of the world’s fastest-growing and most important new sources of energy supply. Suez Canal Authority/Handout via REUTERS Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to the shorter route between Asia and Europe. The carriers announced Monday that their AE1, AE2 and AE3 services will shift from sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to transiting the Suez Canal, with the changes taking effect between December 2026 and January 2027. The announcement builds on a series of earlier routing changes as the partners progressively restore Suez transits across their shared network. According to Maersk’s November 16 advisory, the transitions will begin with the AE2 service on December 4, followed by AE3 on December 20 and AE1 on January 14, 2027. The AE2 service, connecting Asia, Europe and the Middle East, will begin its revised rotation with the Mary Maersk departing from Ningbo. The AE3 service will follow with the Alette Maersk from Shanghai, while the AE1 transition will begin with the Damietta Express, also from Shanghai. The decision follows a broader return to the Suez corridor that has gathered momentum in recent months. In September, the two carriers announced the rerouting of four additional Gemini services — AE5, AE11, AE12 and ME2 — joining two services already using the canal. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd also announced the return of their ME1 service connecting India and Europe, with the first revised sailings scheduled for November 4 and 13. The latest changes extend that shift to more of the carriers’ main Asia-Europe services, reducing reliance on the significantly longer route around southern Africa. For container lines and shippers, the Suez route offers shorter voyages, lower fuel consumption and faster transit times compared with Cape of Good Hope diversions. Returning services to the canal can also free up vessel capacity that has been tied up by longer voyages. Still, the carriers stressed that the return remains dependent on regional security conditions. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said they will continue closely monitoring developments in the Middle East, with any further changes to the Gemini network dependent on continued stability in the Red Sea. The announcement underscores the industry’s growing willingness to restore regular Suez Canal operations, while stopping short of suggesting that security risks in the region have disappeared. articles.title: Saronic taps Syncrolift for Port Alpha Shiplift
articles.summary: Saronic Technologies has selected Norway-based Syncrolift to design and supply what is expected to be the world's largest shiplift and vessel transfer system for Port Alpha, its planned $3 billion shipyard development in Brownsville, Texas.The contract…
articles.body: Saronic taps Syncrolift for Port Alpha Shiplift Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 Rolf-Atle Tomassen, Managing Director of Syncrolift AS; Chris Brinkley, VP of International at Saronic; and Ole Falk Hansen, CEO of Nekkar ASA, commemorated the signing of the shiplift contract in Oslo on November 11, 2026, on the sidelines of the Atlantic Future Forum. Image courtesy Saronic Saronic Technologies has selected Norway-based Syncrolift to design and supply what is expected to be the world's largest shiplift and vessel transfer system for Port Alpha, its planned $3 billion shipyard development in Brownsville, Texas. The contract, valued at more than $100 million, calls for a shiplift featuring a 300-meter platform and lifting capacity of 67,000 tonnes, more than twice the capacity of the next-largest installation, according to Saronic. The system will serve as a centerpiece of Port Alpha's production strategy, which emphasizes high-throughput construction of autonomous and conventionally crewed vessels for commercial and defense customers. Rather than relying on traditional graving docks, Port Alpha will employ a production model allowing multiple ships to be assembled and outfitted simultaneously on land before being transferred to the shiplift for launching. Syncrolift's tandem lifting system will incorporate a rigid platform, condition-monitoring technology and digital-twin controls to support safe vessel movements and lifting operations. "Syncrolift's technology and track record made them the right supplier to deliver a system that is strategically important to how we're approaching Port Alpha and the reindustrialization of U.S. shipbuilding," said Doug Lambert, Saronic Co-Founder and COO. The Port Alpha development initially encompasses 835 acres, with potential expansion to nearly 4,400 acres. Saronic projects the shipyard could create up to 10,000 direct jobs. Syncrolift will manage the project from its headquarters in Vestby, Norway. The award was announced in conjunction with the Atlantic Future Forum, highlighting Saronic's strategy of incorporating technologies and equipment from allied nations into its U.S. shipbuilding operations. The investment reflects Saronic's ambition to increase domestic shipbuilding capacity through automated production processes, advanced vessel-handling infrastructure and parallel construction methods intended to accelerate deliveries.

articles.title: ICS: Geopolitical Tensions Threaten Global Shipping, Freedom of Navigation
articles.summary: The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) has warned that escalating geopolitical tensions, regional conflicts and increasing regulatory fragmentation threaten freedom of navigation and the stability of global maritime trade.Speaking at the…
articles.body: ICS: Geopolitical Tensions Threaten Global Shipping, Freedom of Navigation Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 16, 2026 ICS Chairman John Denholm. Image courtesy ICS The International Chamber of Shipping (ICS) has warned that escalating geopolitical tensions, regional conflicts and increasing regulatory fragmentation threaten freedom of navigation and the stability of global maritime trade. Speaking at the third Hong Kong Global Maritime Trade Summit on November 16, ICS Chairman John Denholm called for renewed international commitment to maritime law and a rules-based trading system, warning that disruptions to established shipping routes and growing protectionism could undermine global supply chains. "We are seeing geopolitical tensions reshape trade flows, conflicts disrupting established shipping routes, greater competition between major economies, and a growing tendency towards unilateral measures and regional regulation," Denholm told more than 250 delegates. He emphasized that shipping, responsible for transporting approximately 90% of global trade by volume, remains fundamental to international economic stability, food security and energy supplies. The summit, organized by ICS in cooperation with Hong Kong's Transport and Logistics Bureau and Hong Kong Shipowners Association, brought together government officials, shipowners and maritime industry executives under the theme "Navigating Risk – Partnering for Resilience." Discussions focused on the economic consequences of maritime disruptions, including rising transportation costs, delayed cargo deliveries and supply chain vulnerabilities. Hong Kong Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan emphasized that strengthening maritime resilience requires cooperation across governments and industries. "In an era of redrawn trade lanes, geopolitical friction and climate urgency, no single jurisdiction or sector can build supply chain resilience alone," Chan said. The summit concluded with calls for stronger international cooperation to protect seafarers, preserve freedom of navigation and maintain reliable global shipping networks. Members meeting in Rome re-elected the Ariston Navigation president and chief executive as chairman for 2027 and 2028, extending a tenure that began in January 2025. Rana, product director of dry cargo operations at Fleet Management, have been elected as two new vice-chairs. The appointments take effect on January 1, 2027. Xylas, who succeeded Dimitrios Fafalios in 2025, will lead an association that has continued expanding its international reach, with membership now exceeding 500 companies and organisations for the first time. Intercargo said its members now operate more than 5,100 dry cargo vessels, up from over 4,500 ships represented at the start of 2026. “We passed 500 members for the first time,” Xylas said, pointing to the association’s growing reach across the world’s major shipping centres. The Rome meeting also approved changes to Intercargo’s structure, including the establishment of a Technical and Operations Committee from January 2027. The new body will bring together technical, operational and vetting activities under the chairmanship of Dimitris Monioudis of Rethymnis & Kulukundis, supported by Cesare d’Api of d’Amico and Psalti. Intercargo has also approved two new working groups focusing on artificial intelligence, digitalisation and crew welfare, which are expected to start work in early 2027. The first production comes less than a month after the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) granted development and production consent for the Jackdaw field off the coast of northeast Scotland to Adura. This project represents £2.1 billion ($2.77 billion) of investment. The company has emphasized that Jackdaw gas will funnel through the existing Shearwater production hub and onwards to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire before being supplied to homes and businesses across Britain. When it reaches peak production in the coming months, the project is expected to produce enough gas to heat the equivalent of around 1.4 million UK homes, helping to reduce Britain’s reliance on imported energy, including liquefied natural gas (LNG), which carries a higher emissions footprint. " Jackdaw is now helping to power Britain. This is a proud moment for everyone at Adura, and a testament to the professionalism, expertise and dedication of our colleagues and the world-class UK supply chain who have worked tirelessly to make it possible. At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. " — Claire Mueller Jackdaw Project Director at Adura The UK operator underlines that Jackdaw will continue to support skilled employment, supply chain businesses, and economic activity throughout its producing life, while generating tax revenues that could help fund public services and investment in net zero projects. According to Adura, the start of production represents the culmination of years of work by skilled people and businesses across the UK, drawing on decades of expertise in the North Sea. Located approximately 250 kilometers east of Aberdeen, this field is expected to be among the lowest-emission developments on the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS), while supporting jobs and bolstering Britain’s energy security. These two projects are expected to generate £1.4 billion ($1.85 billion) in tax revenues before the end of this Parliament, rising to £3.8 billion ($5.02 billion) by the end of the next. It is a positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea and among the skilled people and businesses who have built this industry over decades. As a British company, headquartered in Aberdeen, Adura is proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades, to some of the highest safety and emissions standards in the world. articles.title: CETO wave energy unit makes a splash at BiMEP
articles.summary: Carnegie Clean Energy has deployed CETO wave energy system's buoyant actuator, the unit's prime mover, at the Biscay Marine Energy Platform...
articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 16, 2026 · 1 minute ago CETO wave energy unit makes a splash at BiMEP NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Carnegie Clean Energy Carnegie Clean Energy has deployed CETO wave energy system's buoyant actuator, the unit's prime mover, at the Biscay Marine Energy Platform (BiMEP) in Spain, as part of the first offshore deployment stage delivered in the ACHIEVE Programme. This initial short campaign aims to validate port and maritime authorization pathways, local supply chain logistics, quayside assembly, towing, and offshore installation operations and will deliver learnings for the next stage of deployment where the full CETO system will be deployed, including grid connection, planned for spring. The CETO buoyant actuator will remain at the offshore site at BiMEP in the Basque Country for a short period before being retrieved and brought back to port at the end of the current weather window. The completion of these activities is also said to unlock key funding milestones and financial support under the ACHIEVE Programme’s funding framework. "Seeing the CETO BA in the water offshore at the BiMEP site is a proud moment for everyone at Carnegie. It has taken a mammoth effort from our team in Bilbao to ensure the Stage 1 deployment has been a success," said Carnegie Chief Executive Officer, Jonathan Fiévez . "Whilst this is just the first stage of offshore campaign, the experience gained from this short deployment has increased our team’s capabilities and put us in a much stronger, more certain position as we push toward our full grid-connected Stage 2 deployment in European spring 2027. This is an ambitious project given the large technology leaps we’re taking so executing it in stages and conducting substantial onshore testing are important to manage risk.” Before deployment, the three modular sections of the buoyant actuator were transported from the local Basque fabricator to the Port of Bilbao, where they were assembled quayside. The buoyant actuator was then lowered by crane into the water and docked alongside the quay ready for transport to site. On November 14, the buoyant actuator was towed from the port to Carnegie’s pre-permitted offshore berth at BiMEP, where it was connected to a bespoke installed mooring and anchor system. Over the winter months, the CETO buoyant actuator will be kept onshore in the port while the power take-off (PTO) modules undergo final onshore testing locally, which includes a series of tests with the PTO modules and the electrical module simulating real ocean conditions to validate mechanical, electrical, control and communications functions. Aibel’s FEED work is expected to continue until late next year, while Kongsberg Maritime has secured a separate contract for the vessel’s safety and automation systems. articles.body: Human Capital November 16, 2026 · 6 minutes ago North Sea strike action escalates as offshore workers intensify pressure on Apache in pay and conditions dispute Apache offshore workers have stepped up industrial action over pay and working conditions, bringing North Sea platforms to a standstill. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Beryl Alpha in North Sea Source: APA Around 170 offshore workers employed by Apache, part of APA Corporation, have embarked on strikes amid an ongoing dispute over pay and working conditions, grinding operations across multiple North Sea platforms to a halt, according to Unite the Union. The technicians and operators are protesting against what the union describes as below-inflation pay offers and a controversial seven-day clawback policy, with the UK's trade union warning that industrial action will continue until the company presents an acceptable offer. Unite, described as Britain’s largest offshore trade union, has disclosed that its members on the Forties Alpha , Forties Bravo , Forties Delta , and Beryl Bravo platforms started strike action at 18:00 on November 13, with the action concluding at 17:59 on November 14. Apache workers on the Forties Charlie , Forties Echo , and Beryl Alpha platforms then began strike action from 06:00 on November 15 until 05:59 on November 16. A protest will take place at Apache’s HQ in Aberdeen from 06:45 until 10:00 o’clock on the same date to coincide with the latest phase of strike action ending. " Our Apache members will continue their action until the company make an acceptable offer to the workers. Let's remember that Apache is part of a global operator making billions of pounds in profit. The workers have their union’s full support in the fight for better jobs, pay and conditions. " — Sharon Graham Unite General Secretary Unite emphasizes that trade union members from all across the UK have also sent thousands of emails to Apache management over the weekend, demanding that the company return to the negotiating table to resolve this dispute and stop "attacking" the workers' pay and conditions. The Apache workers emphatically backed strike action in a pay dispute relating to a rejected pay offer, which the UK’s trade union describes as amounting to a real terms pay cut for many workers, ranging from a pay freeze to below-inflation increases. Apache’s parent company, APA Corporation, reported in August $1.7 billion of net cash provided by operating activities, or approximately £1.25 billion, and $738 million of free cash flow, or around £558 million. Unite, which claims to represent workers at Apache who earn significantly below the industry average for their job roles, highlights that the company also operates a detrimental seven-day ‘claw back’ policy, which is above the industry average, forcing workers to complete days of work without extra pay. The offshore workers involved in the strike action include electrical, instrument, mechanical, and production technicians alongside telecoms technicians and radio operators. The previous rounds of strike action in late October and early November brought all seven offshore assets involved in the dispute to a standstill.
